hook.question: A rumour starts with one student. Every hour, everyone who knows it tells all their friends. Who hears it in hour 1, hour 2, hour 3?
paragraphs: Hour 1 is the starter's friends. Hour 2 is those friends' friends who haven't heard it yet. Each hour is one ring around the starter, and the hour you hear the rumour is exactly how many friendship steps you are from them.

Now explore a cave instead. Take a tunnel, then the next unexplored tunnel, then the next, until you hit a dead end. Only then do you walk back to the last fork and try the tunnel you skipped. Same tunnels, but a completely different order of visits.
hook.aha: Both are one loop: take something off a to-do pile, add its unseen neighbours, repeat. Only the choice of what to take next differs. Take the oldest (a queue) and the search spreads in rings and finds the fewest steps: that's BFS. Take the newest (a stack) and it dives deep, then backs up: that's DFS.

parts.title: Grid: distance from S, written in each cell

metaphor: BFS is a ripple in a pond. It reaches everything one step away, then everything two steps away, then three, one full ring at a time.
DFS is a maze explorer trailing a ball of string. Follow one corridor as far as it goes, and at a dead end wind the string back to the last junction that still has a way you haven't tried.
mentalModel.click: Both pull the next cell off a to-do pile and never visit a cell twice. Take the oldest and you spread in rings; take the newest and you dive deep.

glossary.definition: Breadth-first search. Visit everything one step away, then everything two steps away, and so on. It keeps its to-do pile in a queue.
Depth-first search. Follow one path as far as it goes, then back up and try the next. Its to-do pile is a stack, or the recursion call stack.
The cells you have discovered but not explored yet. In BFS these are exactly the cells waiting in the queue.
A record of which cells you have already seen. Check it before queueing a cell so nothing is queued twice and a loop can't trap you.
A queue hands back the oldest item (first in, first out). A stack hands back the newest (last in, first out). That one choice turns the same loop into BFS or DFS.
All the cells at the same distance from the start. BFS finishes one level completely before it starts the next.
The path with the fewest steps when every step counts the same. BFS finds it because it reaches each cell by its fewest steps first. If steps have different costs, plain BFS can be wrong.
A group of nodes that can all reach each other. One search from any node visits exactly its component, so start a new search at each unvisited node to count components.

mentalModel.definition: BFS and DFS visit every node reachable from a start node exactly once, in O(V + E) time (O(R·C) on an R × C grid). They differ only in order. BFS takes the oldest discovered node next, using a queue, so it visits nodes in order of distance and finds fewest-step paths in unweighted graphs. DFS takes the newest, using a stack or recursion, so it follows one path as deep as it can and then backtracks. Both keep a visited set, so extra space is O(V) in general. On a tree there is no visited set to keep: BFS holds one level at a time, O(width), while DFS holds one root-to-node path, O(height).

useWhen: You need the fewest steps, moves or hops and every step costs the same: a maze, a word ladder, a knight's moves.
You must visit everything reachable from a start: count islands, flood-fill a region, find a connected group.
Something spreads outward from one or many places at once, minute by minute, like rotting oranges or the distance to the nearest 0.
The problem hides a graph: grid cells with four neighbours, words one letter apart, puzzle states one move apart.
notWhen: Steps have different costs, like roads with distances or flights with prices. Plain BFS counts steps, not total cost. That is weighted shortest path, so reach for Dijkstra, which swaps the queue for a heap.
You are picking the best answer from overlapping subproblems, like fewest coins or longest increasing run. Nothing is being searched, so dynamic programming fits.
You must build every subset or arrangement and undo choices as you go. That is backtracking: a recursion pattern that dives like DFS but explores choices, not a given graph.

quiz.problem: Given a grid of '1' (land) and '0' (water), count how many separate islands there are.
quiz.explanation: Land cells that touch form a connected component. Scan the grid, and each time you meet unvisited land, count one island and flood the whole island with a search so you never count it again.

quiz.problem: A road map gives the length of every road. Find the shortest total distance from city A to city B.
quiz.explanation: The roads have different lengths, so plain BFS (which counts roads, not kilometres) can pick a worse route. Dijkstra's algorithm fixes this by using a priority queue, which is a heap, to always expand the closest city next.

quiz.problem: Given two words and a dictionary, find the fewest single-letter changes that turn one word into the other, using only dictionary words.
quiz.explanation: Each word is a node, and two words are joined if they differ by one letter. Every change costs one, so the fewest changes is the shortest path, and BFS finds it by trying all 1-change words, then all 2-change words.

quiz.problem: Given an array of distinct numbers, return every possible subset.
quiz.explanation: There is no graph to search. You build each subset by choosing to include or skip each number, and undo the choice to try the other branch. That is recursion with backtracking.

quiz.problem: You can climb 1 or 2 stairs at a time. How many different ways are there to reach the top of an n-step staircase?
quiz.explanation: The ways to reach step n are the ways to reach n - 1 plus the ways to reach n - 2. Overlapping subproblems with a count as the answer call for dynamic programming, not a graph search.

pseudocode.text: dist = a table of −1 (−1 means not seen yet)
while the queue is not empty:
cell = take the front of the queue
if cell is E: return dist[cell]
for each neighbour: up, right, down, left:
if off the grid, a wall, or dist != −1: skip it
add neighbour to the back of the queue

template.time: O(R·C) on an R × C grid, or O(V + E) in a general graph
template.space: O(R·C) for the distance table, or O(V) in a general graph
notes: Stamp a cell when you queue it, not when you pop it. Stamping late lets several neighbours queue the same cell, which bloats the queue and can make the search far slower.

The dist table is both the answer and the visited set: −1 means unseen. It also leaves the input grid untouched. Many solutions overwrite the grid with a marker to save memory; that is only fine when you are allowed to change the input.

Space, precisely: the queue holds one frontier. On a tree that is O(width) for BFS against O(height) of recursion for DFS. On a general graph or grid the visited set is O(V) (O(R·C)) either way, so quote O(V) overall.
Swap the queue for a stack (or recursion) and you get DFS. It still visits each node once in O(V + E), but the first path it finds is not guaranteed to be shortest.
For several starting points, such as every rotten orange or every 0, put them all in the queue at distance 0 before the loop. That is multi-source BFS: one search, many ripples starting together.

examples.title: Flood Fill
examples.problem: You are given an image as a grid of colours, a starting pixel (sr, sc) and a new colour. Repaint the starting pixel and every pixel connected to it up, down, left or right that has the same original colour. Return the repainted image.
approach: Remember the starting colour, old. The area to repaint is every pixel reachable from the start through pixels that still have the colour old.
Recurse: repaint this pixel, then try the four neighbours. Stop at the edge or at any pixel whose colour is not old.
If old already equals the new colour, return early. Otherwise a repainted pixel still looks like old and the recursion never stops.
Work on a copy of the image so the caller's grid is not changed. The pixel at (2,2) is not connected to the start through 1s, so it stays 1.
examples.space: O(R·C) for the recursion in the worst case

examples.title: Number of Islands
examples.problem: Given a grid of '1' (land) and '0' (water), return the number of islands. An island is land joined up, down, left or right, and the edges of the grid count as water.
approach: Scan every cell. Land you have not seen yet must belong to an island nobody has counted, so add one to the count.
Right then, run a DFS from that cell and mark every connected land cell as seen. The whole island is now used up.
Keep a separate seen table. Many solutions flip '1' to '0' instead, which quietly changes the input grid.
Here the scan finds the top-left block, then the single cell at (2,2), then the pair in the bottom-right: 3 islands. Each cell is visited a constant number of times.
examples.space: O(R·C) for the seen table and recursion

examples.title: Rotting Oranges
examples.problem: A grid has 0 (empty), 1 (fresh orange) and 2 (rotten orange). Every minute, each fresh orange next to a rotten one becomes rotten. Return the minutes until no fresh orange is left, or -1 if that never happens.
approach: Every rotten orange spreads at the same time, so this is a BFS that starts from all of them. Put every 2 in the queue at minute 0 and count the fresh oranges.
Each ring of the BFS is one minute. When a fresh orange is reached, write its minute (its parent's minute + 1) and take one off the fresh count.
Here minute 1 rots (0,1) and (1,0), minute 2 rots (0,2) and (1,1), minute 3 rots (2,1), and minute 4 rots (2,2). The last minute written is 4.
If the queue empties while some orange is still fresh, a wall of empty cells blocked it, so the answer is -1.

conceptQuiz.question: You want the fewest steps from S to E in a maze where every step costs the same. Why does BFS find them?
options: It tries every path and keeps the shortest.
It reaches cells in order of distance, so the first time it reaches E is by a shortest route.
It always walks straight toward E.
It needs less memory than DFS.
conceptQuiz.explanation: The queue releases every distance-d cell before any distance-(d + 1) cell, so E is first reached with the fewest steps. It never has to compare paths.

conceptQuiz.question: BFS pops a cell whose distance is 3 and finds an open neighbour that has not been seen. What gets written on that neighbour?
conceptQuiz.explanation: The neighbour is one step further than the cell you popped, so it gets 3 + 1 = 4. This is why BFS distances grow by exactly one per ring.

conceptQuiz.question: DFS reaches E and stops. What do you know about the path it followed?
options: It is a valid path, but not necessarily the shortest.
It is the shortest path, as long as the grid has no walls.
conceptQuiz.explanation: DFS takes the first route it stumbles on, which can twist all over the grid. To guarantee the shortest, DFS would have to try every path and compare, which can take exponential time. BFS needs one pass.

conceptQuiz.question: What goes wrong if BFS marks a cell as seen only when it is popped, instead of when it is queued?
options: Nothing changes: the work is identical.
It returns wrong distances every time.
Several neighbours can queue the same cell, so the queue bloats and the search can slow badly.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Until a cell is popped it still looks unseen, so each neighbour that touches it queues it again. The answer can still be right, but the extra copies waste time and memory.

conceptQuiz.question: Both BFS and DFS run on a general graph with V nodes. What extra memory do both need in the worst case?
options: BFS needs O(V) and DFS needs O(1).
A visited set that can grow to O(V).
BFS needs O(V) and DFS needs O(E).
Only O(1): they just follow edges.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Without a visited set a cycle would loop forever, so both remember every node they have seen: O(V). On a tree (no cycles) you can drop it, and then BFS holds one level, O(width), while DFS holds one path, O(height).

practice.title: Find if Path Exists in Graph
practice.insight: Build neighbour lists from the edges, then search from the source. If the destination ever gets visited, a path exists.

practice.title: Max Area of Island
practice.insight: It is the island counter again, but each search also returns how many cells it used. Keep the biggest.

practice.title: Shortest Path in Binary Matrix
practice.insight: Plain grid BFS, but a step may go to any of 8 neighbours. Count cells on the path, not moves between them.

practice.title: 01 Matrix
practice.insight: Searching from every 1 is slow. Flip it: queue all the 0s at distance 0 and let one BFS ripple outward.

practice.title: As Far from Land as Possible
practice.insight: Start the ripples from all land cells at once. The last water cell the BFS reaches is the farthest one.

practice.title: Surrounded Regions
practice.insight: Ask which O cells can escape: those touching the border through other Os. Search inward from the border first, then flip what's left.

practice.title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
practice.insight: Don't test every cell. Search uphill from each ocean's coast, then keep the cells both oceans reach.

practice.title: Word Ladder
practice.insight: Words are nodes and one-letter changes are edges. Fewest changes is shortest path; generate neighbours by swapping each letter.
